« Les gens ne connaissaient pas les qual: “People didn’t know the qualities of Montréal-Nord’s families,” Samah Aggoun tells us. For the mother of four, it’s the families who make the neighbourhood beautiful and dynamic. And here, there’s no shortage of families. “There are a lot of advantages to living in Montréal-Nord. There’s a way of life,” says Samah, describing the lively community, the spirit of mutual aid and the kindness of the neighbours. That’s why she feels at home in Montréal-Nord. “We love life, we love to give, we have to find a plan.”
Ce matin, Samah participe à une activité: This morning, Samah is taking part in a food assistance activity. She hasn’t yet had a moment to eat breakfast and drink her coffee, but her good mood and energy are contagious. Later, before her hospital appointment, she’ll drop off two baskets of fruits and vegetables at families’ homes along the way. Samah is part of the Montréal-Nord moms’ committee. Very active, she’s also involved in other neighbourhood initiatives. But this one is different: it isn’t a program or an organization, and its members aren’t activists. The neighbourhood’s parents are demanding change.
« Pourquoi les mamans ? Ce sont souvent: “Why moms? It’s often women who are out front,” Samah believes. They have front-row seats to the problems, but above all, they’re the ones who go out and seek solutions.
Les mères du quartier se sont rassemblée: The neighbourhood’s mothers came together to draft a petition and bring it to the National Assembly. They are asking for more resources and help for young people and their parents, who have few alternatives available to them. Recent incidents and the current climate, made worse by COVID, are hitting the borough’s population particularly hard. Residents, like the organizations that help them, are running out of steam. The Montréal-Nord moms’ committee is asking for investment in the community by taking care of young people and families so that the neighbourhood can flourish.
À l’origine de cette mobilisation, il y: This mobilization began with a heartfelt plea from one mom following the tragic events of July 24, 2019, when gunshots rang out in a neighbourhood alley in the middle of the afternoon. On October 25, 2019, Abderrahmane Hadj-Ahmed, a 23-year-old man, lost his life in an alley in the neighbourhood after being struck by a bullet. Some 30 moms answered the call and began meeting. “Families are very worried about their young people’s future,” says Samah.
À Montréal-Nord, le taux de chômage des: In Montréal-Nord, the unemployment rate among young people under 30 is almost twice as high as in the rest of the province. Low-income families with a child aged 0 to 5 make up more than half of the population in the northeast of the borough.
Samah dénonce le manque de services dans: Samah denounces the lack of services in the neighbourhood and wants to see accessible initiatives appear that are adapted to participants’ ages. She also wants parents’ voices to be heard, and for them to be consulted and included in decision-making processes.
« Il faut commencer jeune, et offrir que: “You have to start young, and offer something to the kids… But also to their moms – we’re tired, we’re exhausted.”The mother, who is heavily involved in neighbourhood life, wants to raise awareness among others about the neighbourhood’s realities.
« Ce qui se passe à Montréal-Nord, on tr: “What’s happening in Montréal-Nord, we find it’s not fair,” she says. She was shocked and surprised to learn that the borough is one of the most disadvantaged places in the country. “As long as it’s like this, we need all levels – municipal, provincial, federal, citizens, police – to come together and work on it to find the solution,” she adds. She also wants words to turn into concrete measures. “Montréal-Nord has become a playground for theories. I want real change on the ground.”
Et elle croit, justement, que les choses: And she believes, in fact, that things will eventually change.
Sonia réside dans le quartier depuis 30: Sonia has lived in the neighbourhood for 30 years. “I grew up here,” she says. She has lived elsewhere, but she always comes back to her first love. “If I ever get a medal one day, it’ll be because I take part in neighbourhood life,” she says, laughing. It’s the camaraderie that keeps her here. While the resident worries about violence, she also fears stigmatization and stereotypes. “We have to stop putting labels on everyone,” the 47-year-old mother pleads. She also wants the perception of the neighbourhood to change.
« J’ai le sentiment que, lorsqu’un événe: “I feel like when something happens in Montréal-Nord, the media paint things as worse than they are,” she says. Louisa, who has lived in Montréal-Nord for more than 20 years, agrees. “When something happens here, the papers have a field day with it, even if these aren’t situations unique to the neighbourhood,” she laments. The resident instead sees Montréal-Nord as a multicultural, lively and diverse neighbourhood where communities rub shoulders. “There’s a special colour, a particular colour, in Montréal-Nord. It’s a good place to live,” she says. She’d like the positive things to be highlighted as much as the rest.
« C’est un quartier comme les autres. Ou: “It’s a neighbourhood like any other. Yes, there are challenges, like exclusion, precarity, unemployment. Help us make things better,” she says. “That’s what I want to see change.”Louisa defends Montréal-Nord heart and soul wherever she goes. The image people give of the borough hurts her deeply, and she hopes it won’t always be this way.
Lorsque ses enfants étaient plus jeunes,: When her children were younger, some of their friends’ parents refused to let their kids spend time in Montréal-Nord. “They said it was dangerous,” she says indignantly. Delivery drivers have also expressed reluctance about going to the neighbourhood.
« On est presque obligés de se cacher. L: “We almost have to hide. Young people looking for work don’t say they’re from Montréal-Nord.” The neighbourhood is young and dynamic. “We have to reinvest here, help young people. We have to believe in them, not let them think they have no future.” She supports the Montréal-Nord moms’ committee.
« C’est surtout les femmes qui se mobili: “It’s mostly women who are mobilizing, because they’re at the heart of daily life. They don’t often dare to speak up, but they have things to say.” Sylvie, a mom from Montréal-NordOutside, on the sidewalk, as the March sun warms the air, Sylvie has just signed the petition. On Lapierre Street, there’s a festive mood for the distribution of free eco-friendly menstrual products, a way to mark International Women’s Day.
« C’est sûr que je donne mon nom pour de: “Of course I put my name down for projects like these, that have an impact,” says Sylvie. She has lived in Montréal-Nord for 24 years, the age of her eldest child. “People are always trying to get me to move, but I love my neighbourhood too much,” she says. “I’m not leaving. There are so many resources that can help us when we’re in a jam, we know where to turn, there are organizations I would never have had access to anywhere else.” What does she most love to see in her neighbourhood?
